newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Players await PPI, payrolls.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Players await PPI, payrolls.

text.p: The prices of U.S. Treasury securities will likely remain rangebound Tuesday ahead of key economic releases due later in the week, analysts said.
Traders said activity ground to a halt on Monday amid a dearth of meaningful new numbers. That and thin trading helped to exaggerate price movements.

"It's absolutely dead," said Cary Leahey, senior economist at Lehman Government Securities. He saw activity remaining muted until Thursday's release of producer price data and Friday's crucial nonfarm payrolls report.
With the exception of remarks to be made at about 820 EST/1320 GMT Tuesday by Federal Reserve Bank of Boston President Cathy Minehan, market participants should have little hard news to trade on.

Several Fed Bank presidents and one governor are slated to speak this week and the markets will pay close attention to their remarks. Looming on February 4 and 5 is the next meeting of the policy-making Federal Open Market Committee.
Fear that a stronger-than-expected jump in nonfarm payrolls in December could help lead to an eventual tightening of interest rates by the Fed weighed on the market.

"There's not a whole lot of anything to trade on Tuesday. We have the retail surveys (BTM Schroder and the Redbook report), but other than that just ... Cathy Minehan," said Dan Seto, economist at Nikko Securities International Inc.
Seto said that while a strong employment report could push the Fed to tighten at its February meeting, a move to tighten was more likely in March.
"Given the strength of some of the large numbers we've seen recently it's always a possibility, but I see very little activity between now and the end of the week," Seto said.

"The retail sales reports may be the type of numbers people look at a little more closely than usual as they cover the Christmas shopping period," said Charles Lieberman, director of financial markets research at Chase Securities. Lieberman said retailers' inventories were fairly lean and strong consumer demand could lead to stepped up production.
He also termed heavy issuance of corporate paper a "small negative" for the Treasury market.
In addition, November factory orders were slated for at 1000 EST/1500 GMT and seen 0.6 percent lower than October.

In late trading Monday the 30-year bond was down 17/32 at 99-15/32 to yield 6.78 percent. The two-year note was down 1/32 at 99-19/32 to yield 5.97 percent. The five-year note was down 3/32 at 99-9/32 to yield 6.29 percent, while the 10-year note was at 99-23/32, down 8/32, to yield 6.54 percent.
Federal funds closed right at the Federal Reserve's current target level of 5.25 percent and were expected to open trade Tuesday between 5-3/16 percent and 5.25 percent.
